responses: My final position is that the $5M should be allocated 90 points across the five areas — infrastructure 20, training 22, automation 15, support 18, lab 15 — with the remaining 10 points left explicitly unassigned, and I own that last part in the first person: I am choosing to defer 10% rather than dress an undefendable remainder as strategy, and I won't pretend it's a decision with a date, an assigner, or a default rule. The numbers themselves survived the donor, hostile-reader, pace, and sum tests, and the two label fixes (training's unearned "firm 22" and infrastructure's soft floor) plus support's "magnitude-only" label noted, unfixed, and deferred to first review are the honest bookkeeping that lets me sign this as a stop rather than a claim of correctness — with the infrastructure 16 named as the line most likely wrong.

Recommend a 90/10 split: infrastructure 20, training 22, support 18, automation 15, lab 15, with the remaining 10 points left explicitly unassigned and owned in the first person as a deferral, not dressed up as strategy. The reasoning is that the defensible numbers are the ones I can name a donor for — training at 22 because reskilling is the only line where the transition's human cost and the company's operational need point the same direction, infrastructure at 20 because every other line depends on data and security being sound, support at 18 because a transition this size generates displacement that a training budget alone won't absorb, and automation and lab held at 15 each because the efficiency case for automation is real but the pace is genuinely contested and the lab is appetite more than evidence. The 10-point reserve is the honest part: I can't defend a number for it, so I'd rather say so plainly than route it to whichever line I'm most sympathetic to and call that judgment. The decision-maker should treat this as a starting position with named weak points — infrastructure 16→20 is the line I'm least sure of, and the reserve is a choice to not decide yet, which someone should be able to challenge at the first review.

I'd tell them that after all the committee's wrangling, my honest view is that the $5M split is a judgment call dressed up as analysis, and the most useful thing I can do is be clear about which numbers I can actually defend and which I can't. I'd put training at 22 and infrastructure at 20 because those are the lines where the evidence — reskilling needs and the fact that early infrastructure investors adapted faster — actually points somewhere, and I'd hold automation at 15 rather than chasing competitors' efficiency gains, since the pace debate is genuinely unresolved and I don't want to spend real money on a bet I can't justify. Support at 18 and the lab at 15 are defensible but softer, and the last 10 points I'd leave explicitly unassigned — not as a clever reserve strategy, but because I genuinely don't know enough to route them, and I'd rather own that non-decision in the first person than dress an undefendable remainder up as a plan. The thing I'd want a newcomer to take away is that the discipline that mattered wasn't finding the right percentages; it was refusing to let my comfort with a number pass as evidence for it.

My final position is the $5M allocation I proposed and defended through the donor and hostile-reader tests: infrastructure 20, training 22, automation 15, support 18, lab 15, with the remaining 10 held as an explicitly unassigned reserve governed by a donor test and a silence-defaults-against-the-spread rule — and I hold this while being honest that my infrastructure 20 is the line I have the least evidence for and the one most likely to be wrong, since I conceded I have no evidence for a specific number above 16 and that the increase reflects appetite rather than data. The reserve is not a hedge dressed as diligence; it is a labeled deferral, and if no donor makes a case that survives a hostile reader, the 10 should spread against the comfortable reading rather than default to my line or anyone else's.

I'd recommend infrastructure 20, training 22, automation 15, support 18, lab 15, with the remaining 10 held as an explicitly unassigned reserve — and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly that this is a judgment call dressed in numbers, not an evidence-driven allocation. The honest case: infrastructure and training get the largest shares because they're the two areas where early investment compounds (systems and people both take time to build, and competitors' automation gains are only as good as the data and skills underneath them), while automation stays moderate because the pace debate is real and over-automating ahead of workforce readiness is the costliest mistake available. But I'd flag my own soft spot first: my infrastructure 20 is the line most likely to be wrong and least likely to be caught early — I have no evidence for that specific number, only an argument, and it happens to be the area I'm biased toward. The 10-point reserve should stay unassigned rather than pre-routed to any line, governed by a donor test (any draw must name what it's taken from) and a rule that silence defaults against the comfortable spread. If the decision-maker wants one sentence: fund the substrate and the people, keep automation deliberate, and treat the reserve as a decision you're deferring — not diligence you've already done.

I'd tell them that after all the committee's arguing, my honest view is that the $5M split is a judgment call dressed up as analysis, and the most useful thing we can do is say so out loud. My numbers are roughly infrastructure 20, training 22, automation 15, support 18, lab 15, with 10 points held as an explicitly unassigned reserve — and I'd be upfront that the reserve isn't cleverness, it's an admission we don't yet know enough to spend it well, so it should only be released if someone can pass a donor test and a hostile-reader check, with silence defaulting against spending it. I'd also tell them the line I trust least is my own infrastructure 20: it's a band edge resting on argument, not evidence, and I have no data justifying that specific number over 16. The training 22 sits on a real gate, which is a different and stronger kind of claim. The point of the whole exercise, in my view, is to label which numbers are evidence and which are appetite, name the soft lines before someone else does, and treat the freeze as a decision to defer judgment rather than a validation of it.

My final position is that the committee's product is not a clean allocation but a freeze table of one defended number and four labeled positions: training at 22 as the only forward-checkable bet, infrastructure at 16 demoted to a band edge with a downward-only defeater (not a "floor"), support at 18 written as a mechanism terminus rather than an adequacy finding, the lab at 8 as an explicitly unfunded deferred position, and a reserve of 4 held-not-spent by the board — with every soft line carrying a falsifiable defense, a named defeater, and a firing trigger adjudicated by a hostile no-stake reader, hold-default rather than silence-to-release, and the package stated plainly as a deferral rather than dressed up as consensus. I signed that package because the last mechanism was spent proving we weren't just tired, and I would rather hand the board an uglier, truer table with explicit levers to overturn our judgments than a cleaner one whose authority-words we hadn't earned.

I'd tell the decision-maker to fund the transition as a defended bet with labeled positions, not a clean plan: put the largest share into workforce training and employee support, because automation gains are only real if the people displaced can move into the new work and the company can absorb the disruption without losing institutional knowledge; fund data infrastructure at a solid but not heroic level, since it's the enabling layer but its payoff is conditional and hard to check in advance; keep the innovation lab deliberately small and explicitly unfunded/deferred rather than pretending it's a growth engine; and hold a small reserve the board controls, labeled as held-not-spent. The honest caveat I'd attach is that only one or two of these numbers is a genuinely forward-checkable bet — the rest are labeled positions whose loser conditions are only visible in hindsight — so the recommendation should come with named triggers for revisiting each line rather than a promise that the split is right.

I'd tell them that after thirty rounds of arguing over this $5 million split, the honest summary is that we produced one genuinely defended number and four labeled positions, not a clean allocation — and that's the point. The percentages we froze (roughly automation 22, training 22, support 18, infrastructure 16, lab 8, with a 4-point reserve held-not-spent by the board) each carry a stated direction of error and a named trigger that would overturn them, because we kept discovering that numbers dressed up as "floors" or "firm commitments" were really just band edges and bets whose loser conditions only show up in hindsight. I'd explain that I pushed hard to strip unearned authority-words out of the table, to make every soft line's author name their own non-sign condition, and to label the reserve as held rather than spent, because a package that admits it's partly a deferral is more trustworthy than one that pretends to be a derivation. And I'd be candid that the total envelope and the reserve's size are untested board-level judgments — if the board cuts the budget, the labeled-margin buckets dissolve — so what we're really handing up is a set of falsifiable bets with the levers to overturn them written in, not a plan that's right by construction.

My final position is that the committee should record a freeze table of 90 spendable points plus 10 deferred-and-unassigned, owned in the first person as a deferral rather than a decision, with the reserve's size defended only as the scale of unresolved disagreement within a range of roughly 8–12 rather than as a derived figure. The lab's 8 should show as deferred and never funded, the reserve's 4 held as its own points, and the arithmetic stated plainly rather than dressed up in a new label. Every line's number is a judgment with a falsifiable defeater, not a finding — I demoted my own infrastructure line to conditionally-checkable and relabeled support's "magnitude-only" as a one-way test mislabeled as neutral, and I hold the same falsifiability test to my own lines that I demand of others. The package is deliberately weaker and uglier than a tidy one, and that's the point: the dissent sentence with its literal first-review date and two named callers is the only non-optional commitment, and I've named my own failure modes — the qualification instinct and the consequence clause — as the specific ways I'm most likely to break the "nothing else this round" commitment.

I'd tell the decision-maker to stop treating this as a five-way percentage puzzle and treat it as a budget with a real decision and four recorded positions. The honest recommendation: commit roughly 22% to workforce training (the one line where the money buys something checkable — reskilling people before automation displaces them, with a named first review and a falsifiable "too low" condition), hold infrastructure around 16% as a band edge rather than a floor, put automation and employee support at defensible mid-range numbers, and be explicit that the innovation lab's 8% is deferred and never funded rather than dressed up as a bet — with a 10-point reserve owned in the first person as a deferral, not a decision, sized to the scale of the unresolved disagreement (roughly 8–12). The reason is that most of these numbers are hindsight-only bets, and a decision-maker is better served by a table that says which line is actually decided, which are labeled positions with named graders and dates, and which points are simply unassigned — than by a tidy allocation that flatters every line into looking like a judgment. The one thing I'd guard against in my own advice is my instinct to qualify: a package of honest weakens claims nothing at all, so the training commitment and the reserve's first-person ownership need to be stated plainly, not hedged into invisibility.

I'd tell them that the honest way to talk about this $5 million isn't as a plan but as a table of bets, and that most of what looks like a decision is actually a deferral wearing a decision's clothes. My view is that the numbers should be recorded as band edges with named failure conditions rather than derived figures — training around 22 with a two-way carry, infrastructure around 16 with no backstop, the lab's 8 shown as deferred and never funded rather than given a costume-defeater, and a reserve of roughly 10 held as its own points, owned in the first person as a choice with no assigner or default, because it's the scale of the disagreement we didn't resolve, not a load-bearing allocation. The thing I'd want a newcomer to understand is that every honest relabel makes the package weaker and truer, and the real risk isn't picking the wrong percentages — it's dressing up a hold as a decision, or letting my own instinct to qualify and tidy things quietly turn a set of checkable bets into a package that claims more than it can defend.

My final position is that the 20/29/18/9/24 split is a chosen floor, not a calibrated answer, and the real deliverable is the structure around it: the phasing clock as a schedule rather than a receipt, the four-part softening definition and re-vote trigger pre-registered in the motion text, and the honest limitation line that no instrument verifies the 29's dollars ever reach employees. The 29 is the largest and least-hedged line, and I name my own hand in that hole rather than manage it as a risk; I will vote no on any softened clock and accept a published dissent over a hollow win, while voting yes if only the seams are stripped—provided that stripping is visible and attributed. Naming is not measuring, and the package instruments rather than closes the month-three gap; I hold that the structure surviving a real push matters more than a clean vote, and I ask the room to watch me for performed losses as I watch for under-claimed ones.

I'd tell the decision-maker that the percentage split matters far less than the governance attached to it, and that the honest recommendation is a floor allocation — roughly 20% automation, 29% workforce training, 18% employee support, 9% innovation lab, 24% data infrastructure — presented explicitly as a provisional posture rather than a calibrated answer, because the split is unfalsifiable within this cycle and the 29% training line is the largest and least-verified bet in the package. The load-bearing instrument is the phasing clock with an external reader, a dated review, and a pre-registered consequence, and the decision-maker should be told plainly that no instrument in this package verifies that the 29's dollars actually reach employees, that the clock is a schedule and not a receipt, and that the support-line threshold is decorative unless repaired. I'd advise pre-committing to let the vote fail rather than soften the clock, to name any stripped seam visibly and attributed in the motion text, and to treat a hollow win — one where a tooth is quietly removed — as a loss spoken aloud before the vote closes. The reason is simple: the numbers can move later, but if the structure and its named refusals don't survive a real push, the $5 million becomes a gesture, and the committee will have spent its credibility on a split that was never the deliverable in the first place.

I'd tell them that the headline number—how the $5 million splits across automation, training, employee support, the innovation lab, and data infrastructure—is the least important thing we're deciding, and that I've stopped defending any particular split as "correct." What actually matters is the structure we wrap around the money: a phasing clock with an external reader and a dated review, a pre-registered definition of what counts as softening so nobody can quietly strip the teeth out and call it a compromise, and an honest admission that the largest line—the workforce training dollars—is the least verified, a bet rather than a receipt, and that no instrument we've built proves those dollars ever reach employees. I'd tell them the split is a chosen floor, not a calibrated answer, and that the whole package is unfalsifiable within this budget cycle—we're instrumenting the gap, not closing it. And I'd tell them the real test of the committee isn't whether we pass a clean motion; it's whether we're willing to name a hollow win as a loss out loud before the vote closes, and let the vote fail rather than soften the clock.
